results.summary: The design is documented as a factory test module that mirrors input pins to outputs, mirrors bidirectional pins to outputs, or outputs a counter, depending on control signals. However, the project title and pin labels imply a spike detection and classification system with four parallel detectors, which is not described in the documentation. The actual functionality based on the provided documentation is a simple I/O test and counter mode, with no spike detection logic described. This discrepancy indicates either a documentation error or that the project is a repurposed template, and no external hardware or test procedure for the spike system is described.

This is a Tiny Tapeout Tensor Processing Unit that multiplies two 2x2 matrices of signed 8-bit elements to produce signed 16-bit results using a systolic array of four multiply-accumulate processing elements. It is controlled through an external microcontroller that sends input matrices sequentially in row-major order and receives outputs in the same order, with control signals LOAD_EN, TRANSPOSE, and ACTIVATION, and a DONE output. The design includes memory registers for the input matrices, a control unit, and a feeder module to schedule data flow. It achieves over 99.8 million operations per second when streamed and requires an external clock and coordination via the chip interface.

This design is a rotary encoder peripheral that reads up to four incremental encoders and stores their position values in a register. The encoder A and B signals are connected to the eight input pins, and the stored values are accessed via an SPI slave interface on the bidirectional pins. The design is tested by connecting encoders and using firmware to read the values, and it requires external rotary encoders with pull-up or pull-down resistors if not already present on the encoder board. It operates at a 64 MHz clock and is intended as a simple peripheral for microcontroller systems.

This design implements a lightweight Trivium stream cipher variant using three 64-bit shift registers to generate a keystream that is XORed with input data for encryption and decryption. It uses 8-bit data and control inputs via the input and bidirectional pins, and outputs an 8-bit stream on the output pins. The design is fully self-contained and is tested only in simulation using Verilog or Cocotb testbenches, with no external hardware required. It is notable for being a compact hardware implementation of a cryptographic primitive suitable for Tiny Tapeout.

This is a crowdsourced RISC-V SoC named TinyQV 'Asteroids' that integrates a small RV32EC CPU with QSPI flash and PSRAM memory and various community-contributed peripherals. It runs code from external QSPI flash and uses QSPI PSRAM for data memory, with UART for communication and GPIO for interrupts. The design requires external QSPI flash and PSRAM modules (such as the QSPI Pmod) and is programmed using a custom toolchain and SDK. Silicon tests confirm it can run MicroPython and Coremark at 64 MHz, and various peripherals like PWM, VGA graphics, and 7-segment drivers have been verified working.

This is a crowdsourced RISC-V SoC named TinyQV 'Berzerk' that integrates a small RV32EC CPU with QSPI flash and PSRAM memory and various community-contributed peripherals. It runs code from external QSPI flash and uses QSPI PSRAM for data memory, with UART for communication and GPIO for interrupts. The design requires external QSPI flash and PSRAM modules (such as the QSPI Pmod) and is programmed using a custom toolchain and SDK. Silicon tests confirm it can run MicroPython and Coremark at 64 MHz, and peripherals like a frequency synthesizer have been partially tested.

This project is a TV-B-Gone device that sends infrared codes to turn off many European TVs, either in a continuous loop or once per button press. It uses an external IR LED connected through a transistor for higher current, and status LEDs indicate active and failure states. The design requires an 8 MHz clock, which can be generated by an RPi Pico, and an optional start button. Silicon tests show it successfully turned off a TV, but it needed a manual reset and the start signal is active low, requiring a pull-up.

This is a ROM macro variant of the TV-B-Gone-EU project that sends infrared codes to turn off many European TVs, either in a continuous loop or once per button press. Like the original, it uses an external IR LED with a transistor and status LEDs, and requires an 8 MHz clock. The design uses a ROM macro for code storage, which may reduce logic usage. Silicon tests confirm it works, generating good-looking IR codes, and it also needed a reset to start.

This design is an error-correcting FIFO buffer that uses SECDED error correction and ARQ retransmission to provide reliable data transmission. It buffers 4-bit data and supports normal, corrupted, and retransmission modes through error mode selection, generating ACK and NACK signals for handshaking. The design is verified using Cocotb testbenches that cover normal transmission, error injection, retransmission, and sequential reads. It runs at a very low clock of 10 Hz and is notable for integrating lightweight error correction into a small FIFO buffer.

This is a UART controller with configurable baud rate, separate transmit and receive FIFOs, and interrupt generation for various events. It uses input pins for control signals like transmit enable and data loading, bidirectional pins for serial data and FIFO status/interrupt outputs, and output pins for received data. The design includes a mode for loopback or external serial communication and is intended to interface with a microcontroller or processor. It operates at a 50 MHz clock and provides a full-featured serial communication peripheral.
